title: Wild versus commercial seed source shapes intraspecific trait variation and drought response in Schizachyrium scoparium
content:
Trait variation in wild-collected and commercially sourced Schizachyrium scoparium was compared under ambient and drought conditions to inform seed sourcing decisions for prairie restoration. Wild plants exhibited a positive relationship between intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE) and biomass retention under drought (lnRR), whereas commercial plants showed no significant relationship, indicating that wild plants may show greater drought resilience.


Abstract

Prairies are refugia of biodiversity, but these ecosystems have been severely degraded. A common restoration approach is the reintroduction of native plants through seeds, but seed sourcing approaches vary, including the use of wild-collected and commercially produced seeds. Commercial seed production offers advantages for restoration, including meeting the seed demands of large projects, generating well-provisioned and more viable seeds compared to stressed wild populations, and mitigating low genetic diversity or inbreeding in small, remnant wild populations. However, commercially produced seeds can face selective pressures that may alter functional traits—the morphological, physiological or phenological characteristics that influence plant performance and ecosystem function—compared to wild-collected seeds. Therefore, the differences between these source types must be understood so that practitioners can make informed seed sourcing decisions for habitat restorations. We examined above- and below-ground traits of three wild-collected and three commercially produced accessions of Schizachyrium scoparium, a native grass used extensively in prairie restoration. Our 6-week drought experiment at the Chicago Botanic Garden investigated how traits, trait variability, trait relationships and drought response vary between source types. All accessions demonstrated intraspecific trait variation (ITV), and wild plants exhibited stronger trait associations with drought response than commercial plants. However, few differences in ITV and trait relationships were found between source types for most traits. This work demonstrates that differences between source types exist, but they are not consistent across all traits or conditions. This reinforces the importance of considering within-species differences, as different source types or populations may respond uniquely to environmental stressors. Practical implication. Our results indicate that commercially produced sources are not consistently functionally distinct from wild-collected sources, suggesting that seed selection should not rely on source type alone. Although commercial sources are valuable for meeting restoration demands and supporting establishment, wild-collected sources should continue to be incorporated when available to maintain variation and adaptive potential within restored populations. Restoration practitioners should incorporate trait information into seed sourcing decisions by using trait data from field trials, published studies or seed suppliers to select plant material with traits and stress responses best suited to site conditions and restoration goals.
